result: L2/3 neurons in mouse auditory cortex (ACx) respond to auditory, visual, and motor-related stimuli. Pure tones evoked diverse individual responses but a net population decrease in activity. Visual gratings evoked diverse responses with an initially positive population response. Running onsets evoked predominantly increased activity at both individual and population levels. Running modulated auditory and visual responses differentially compared to V1.
evaluation: Claims C2-C10, C13-C14, C18, and C84 are well-supported by calcium imaging data showing responses to all three stimulus types (Figures 1F-N). The characterization includes both individual neuron diversity and population-level statistics with appropriate controls. The differential running modulation compared to V1 is supported by comparison to cited prior work (C12, C15).

result: L2/3 neurons in ACx respond to audiomotor (AM) mismatches in a manner similar to visuomotor (VM) mismatch responses in V1. AM mismatch neurons exhibit opposing influences of auditory (inhibitory) and motor-related (excitatory) inputs, consistent with subtractive computation of prediction errors. The AM mismatch response was present from the first exposure session and was significantly stronger than sound offset responses in open-loop playback.
evaluation: Claims C19-C25, C28-C30, C33-C38, C40-C41, C87, and C90 are supported by experimental data showing strong population responses to AM mismatches (Figure 2C-D), opposing correlations with sound amplitude (negative) and running speed (positive) in AM mismatch neurons (Figure 2G), and differences between closed and open loop conditions (Figure 2H). The comparison to V1 VM mismatch responses is supported by citations to prior work (C35, C88-C89).

result: There is no evidence of visuomotor (VM) mismatch responses at the population level in L2/3 ACx. While a small subset of neurons (5%) showed responses to VM mismatches, these neurons did not differ from the general population in their responses to visual stimuli or running onsets, and showed random correlations with visual flow and running speed. Running onset responses were not different between closed and open loop conditions.
evaluation: Claims C44-C54 are supported by experimental data showing no significant population response to VM mismatches (Figure 3C-D), no differences between VM mismatch-responsive neurons and the rest of the population (Figure 3E-F), random correlation distributions (Figure 3G), and no difference in running onset responses between conditions (Figure 3H). The lack of population-level response is a negative result but is well-controlled and clearly demonstrated.

result: Concurrent audiomotor and visuomotor [AM + VM] mismatches elicit responses in ACx that are significantly larger than either mismatch alone and exceed the linear sum of individual mismatch responses. A subset of neurons (13.7%) selectively responds to concurrent mismatches, while another subset (11.2%) responds preferentially to isolated mismatches. This demonstrates non-linear, multimodal interactions in prediction error computation.
evaluation: Claims C55-C64, C114, and C118 are supported by experimental data showing super-additive responses to concurrent mismatches compared to both individual mismatches (Figure 4D) and their linear sum (Figure 4E). The identification of distinct neuronal subpopulations with selective responses (Figure 4F) provides strong evidence for non-linear integration. The magnitude of the effect (~2-fold difference) and the presence of selectively responsive neurons support the conclusion of non-linear multimodal interactions.

result: The authors propose that sensorimotor prediction error computation via subtractive interactions between bottom-up and top-down inputs may be a canonical cortical computation in L2/3 that generalizes beyond V1 to other primary cortices. They argue that hierarchical variants of predictive processing are insufficient to explain the observed multimodal interactions and that non-hierarchical models are needed.
evaluation: Claims C42-C43, C91-C92, and C112-C113, C116-C117 represent speculative generalizations and theoretical interpretations. While the data showing similar patterns in ACx and V1 (C90) and non-linear multimodal interactions (C59, C62) provide support, the claims about canonical computation across cortex (C43, C92) and the necessity of non-hierarchical models (C113, C117) extend beyond what the current data can definitively establish. These are reasonable interpretations but require additional evidence from other cortical areas and direct testing of alternative models.

result: AM mismatch responses in ACx appear more sustained than VM mismatch responses in V1, and sound playback halt responses are weaker than in V1 with no running modulation. The authors speculate this may be due to additional sounds generated during running on the treadmill that reduce the salience of experimental sound halts.
evaluation: Claims C93-C97 identify differences between ACx and V1 mismatch responses. While C93-C94 are supported by data (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), the explanations offered in C95-C97 are speculative. The authors acknowledge they have no explanation for the sustained responses (C93) and offer only speculation about treadmill-generated sounds (C95-C96). These observations are valid but the mechanistic explanations remain uncertain.

result: The authors suspect their recorded population is enriched for mismatch neurons because mismatch responses are likely enriched in superficial L2/3 and their two-photon imaging preferentially recorded from more superficial neurons.
evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by citation to prior work showing enrichment of mismatch responses in superficial L2/3 (C31, O'Toole et al., 2023) and the authors' description of their recording approach. This interpretation is consistent with the strong population-level AM mismatch response observed (C20) and the negative population response to sounds (C4).

result: The authors note that a similar non-linear relationship between auditory and visual oddball responses has been described in prior work. They acknowledge that calcium imaging has limitations for assessing non-linearity in spiking responses, but argue the magnitude of their effect (~2-fold) and selective neuronal responses suggest underlying spiking responses are also non-linear.
evaluation: Claims C98-C100 appropriately contextualize the findings with prior work (C98, Shiramatsu et al., 2021), acknowledge methodological limitations (C99), and provide reasonable inference about underlying spiking activity (C100) based on the magnitude of the calcium imaging effect and the presence of selectively responsive neurons. The inference in C100 is speculative but well-justified.

result: The authors speculate about potential mechanisms underlying multimodal mismatch interactions, considering long-range cortico-cortical input from V1, noradrenergic signals from locus coeruleus, and cholinergic signals. They conclude that long-range V1 input interacting with local AM mismatch computation is the most likely mechanism, while neuromodulatory contributions remain uncertain.
evaluation: Claims C101-C111 are largely speculative mechanistic interpretations. While they are grounded in known anatomy and prior work (C102, C104, C105, C108, C109), the specific mechanisms proposed (C103, C106, C107, C110, C111) are not directly tested in this study. The reasoning is logical and appropriately cautious, but these remain hypotheses requiring future experimental validation.

result: Running modulates auditory and visual responses in ACx differently than in V1. In V1, running strongly increases visual responses, while in ACx running modulates auditory responses in various ways and visual responses show running-dependent increases and sitting-dependent decreases similar to V1.
evaluation: Claims C11-C12, C15-C17, C85-C86 are supported by citations to multiple prior studies (C11, C12, C85, C86) and the authors' own data comparing responses during sitting and running (C13-C14, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The comparison to V1 is appropriate and well-supported by prior literature.

result: There is no evidence of running modulation of sound playback halt responses in ACx, in contrast to visual playback halt responses in V1 which show running modulation.
evaluation: Claims C26-C27 are supported by experimental data showing no difference in playback halt responses between sitting and running in ACx (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) and citation to prior work showing running modulation in V1 (C27, Vasilevskaya et al., 2023). This is a clear negative result with appropriate controls.

result: The study used C57BL/6 female mice aged 7-12 weeks, with cranial window surgery at 7-8 weeks. The AM closed loop coupling had a delay of 260±60 ms and VM coupling had a delay of 90±10 ms. The study recorded from 7637 neurons in 17 mice.
evaluation: Claims C119-C123 describe methodological details that are clearly stated in the Methods section. These are factual descriptions of the experimental design and sample size.

result: The authors provide extensive background on prediction errors in cortex, predictive processing theory, motor-related signals, and the anatomical connections between ACx and V1. They note that hierarchical predictive processing models do not account for lateral connections between primary sensory areas.
evaluation: Claims C1, C65-C83, C88-C89, C124-C125 are background claims supported by citations to prior work. These establish the theoretical framework and prior knowledge that motivates the current study. The citations appear appropriate and the characterizations of prior work are reasonable.

result: The circuit mechanisms underlying multimodal integration of mismatch responses are still unclear and require further investigation.
evaluation: Claim C115 is a straightforward acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study. While the authors demonstrate multimodal interactions, they appropriately note that the underlying circuit mechanisms remain to be determined.

result: Sustained running onset responses in open loop possibly reflect motor-related input that is not cancelled out by sensory input.
evaluation: Claim C39 is a speculative interpretation of the sustained responses observed in open loop conditions (C38). While this interpretation is consistent with the predictive processing framework, it is not directly tested and remains a hypothesis.
